text: Book II of the Republic contains two arguments that later readers have often treated separately. The first builds a city from scratch, and Socrates does not present the exercise chiefly as political theory. He presents it as a way of seeing the soul at a larger scale: the city serves as a magnified image of the person (Republic, Book II). The second argument sets rules for what may be said about the gods, and in that argument Plato enters a quarrel already about two hundred years old. Homer and Hesiod were the closest thing ancient Greece had to scripture, and their gods lied, lusted, fought members of their own families, and handed out good and evil from two jars. Xenophanes, the sixth-century BCE philosopher, had mocked those portrayals of the gods. The Athenian jury that condemned Socrates in 399 BCE charged him with impiety and with corrupting the young. Plato’s answer is to make the founders of his city theologians before they are lawgivers. In the Republic, they decide what a god must be before they decide what children may hear. Aristotle would later dispute the founding premise that a city is a remedy for human neediness. For Aristotle, the city is something natural to human beings.
